newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN rights envoy calls for change in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: UN rights envoy calls for change in Iraq.

text.p: A U.N. investigator called on Friday for fundamental change in Iraq, blaming President Saddam Hussein for "long-standing, widespread and systematic violation of human rights".

"Fundamentally, there is no rule of law in Iraq, with all power concentrated in the hands of the president who -- through a complex, vast and infamous security apparatus which he controls -- conducts life in Iraq as he wishes," Max van der Stoel told the U.N. Human Rights Commission.

"Fundamentally, the politico-legal order must change," said van der Stoel, a former Dutch Foreign Minister who has been allowed into Iraq only once in the six years he has served as U.N. rapporteur on the Gulf War's defeated power.
And speaking later to reporters, van der Stoel said: "...This is really one of the worst dictatorships that the world knows at present. It is one of the most dreadful regimes since 1945."
The U.N. forum is expected to condemn Iraq on Tuesday.

The investigator drew a sharp attack from Iraq's delegation. "The special rapporteur's report is a mere duplication of his previous reports, full of allegations and false accusations which only reflect hostile political attitudes against Iraq aiming at fragmenting Iraq and its national unity," said Mohamad Abdullah Al-Douri.
Van der Stoel also urged the U.N. to make sure that food and medical supplies send to Iraq under a deal allowing limited oil exports were not used as a "political weapon" against Saddam's opponents

"I can only express the hope that Iraq will not try to use the food rationing system... to try to give preferential treatment to specific categories of the population and to withhold provision of food to other categories," he said.
"The food rationing system makes it easy for instance to withhold food from a specific tribe which is suspected to be hostile towards the regime," van der Stoel said.

The scheme provides for U.N. monitors to ensure distribution. "Only this can ensure that in a country like Iraq, the food now being distributed via ration cards will not being used by the Iraqi regime as a political weapon," he said.
He said the Iraqi people faced a "famine-like situation" but argued that it had not been necessary for their government to let this happen.
"All those children could still be alive if Iraq had done four years earlier what it has done now at long last, that is to come to agreement under this 'oil-for-food' scheme," he said.
